validated_results.title: Impact of alcohol consumption on the risk of developing bladder cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
validated_results.reason: The article is explicitly a systematic review and meta-analysis of published epidemiologic studies rather than an original primary study.

validated_results.title: Alcohol Drinking and Bladder Cancer Risk From a Pooled Analysis of Ten Cohort Studies in Japan.
validated_results.reason: Pooled analysis of ten Japanese population-based prospective cohorts reporting incident bladder cancer risk for alcohol drinking with a target hazard ratio.

extraction.comparison_type: Men consuming alcohol ≥69 g/week vs reference drinking category
extraction.design: Pooled analysis of prospective cohort studies
extraction.population: Japanese participants in ten population-based prospective cohort studies

sample_size.excerpt: The aim of this study was to examine the association between alcohol drinking and bladder cancer risk using data from ten population-based prospective cohort studies in Japan, where approximately 40% of the population has inactive ALDH2 enzyme. We analyzed 340,497 Japanese participants with average follow-up of 13.4 years.

cases.excerpt: During 4,729,071 person-years, 936 men and 325 women were newly diagnosed with bladder cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: Our results showed no evidence of significant association between alcohol drinking and bladder cancer risk even among men who consumed alcohol of ≥69 g/week, with HR of 1.02 (95% CI, 0.79-1.33).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Our results showed no evidence of significant association between alcohol drinking and bladder cancer risk even among men who consumed alcohol of ≥69 g/week, with HR of 1.02 (95% CI, 0.79-1.33).

comparison.excerpt: among men who consumed alcohol of ≥69 g/week

design.excerpt: using data from ten population-based prospective cohort studies in Japan

continent.excerpt: ten population-based prospective cohort studies in Japan

exposure_measurement.excerpt: The association between alcohol drinking and bladder cancer risk was evaluated using Cox regression models within each study

gender.excerpt: among men who consumed alcohol of ≥69 g/week

validated_results.title: Intake of milk and other dairy products and the risk of bladder cancer: a pooled analysis of 13 cohort studies.
validated_results.reason: Pooled cohort analysis reporting a dairy-specific hazard ratio for incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest tertile of total 'other' dairy product consumption
extraction.population: Participants of 13 cohort studies in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study

sample_size.excerpt: Thirteen cohort studies, included in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study, provided data for 3590 BC cases and 593,637 non-cases.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 3590 + 593637 = 597227

cases.excerpt: Thirteen cohort studies, included in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study, provided data for 3590 BC cases and 593,637 non-cases.

effect_size.excerpt: Overall, total 'other' dairy product consumption was not associated with BC risk (HR comparing highest with lowest tertile: 0.97 (95% CI: 0.87-1.07; p<sub>trend</sub> = 0.52) and likewise no association was observed for either liquid milk, processed milk, cream, cheese or icecream.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Overall, total 'other' dairy product consumption was not associated with BC risk (HR comparing highest with lowest tertile: 0.97 (95% CI: 0.87-1.07; p<sub>trend</sub> = 0.52) and likewise no association was observed for either liquid milk, processed milk, cream, cheese or icecream.

validated_results.title: Intake of milk and other dairy products and the risk of bladder cancer: a pooled analysis of 13 cohort studies.
validated_results.reason: The pooled cohort analysis provides a separable yoghurt (fermented dairy food) estimate for incident bladder cancer risk.

extraction.comparison_type: Moderate yoghurt consumption (25-85 g/day) versus non-consumers
extraction.population: Participants of 13 cohort studies in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study

sample_size.excerpt: Thirteen cohort studies, included in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study, provided data for 3590 BC cases and 593,637 non-cases.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 3590 + 593637 = 597227

cases.excerpt: Thirteen cohort studies, included in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study, provided data for 3590 BC cases and 593,637 non-cases.

effect_size.excerpt: However, an inverse association was observed between yoghurt consumption and BC risk when comparing those in the moderate (25-85 g/day) and high categories (>85 g/day) with non-consumers, with multivariate HR of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.75-0.96) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.78-0.98), respectively. We found no evidence of association between either total or individual dairy products and BC risk, but suggestive evidence that consumption of yoghurt may be associated with a decreased risk.

confidence_interval.excerpt: However, an inverse association was observed between yoghurt consumption and BC risk when comparing those in the moderate (25-85 g/day) and high categories (>85 g/day) with non-consumers, with multivariate HR of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.75-0.96) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.78-0.98), respectively.

validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Prospective Netherlands Cohort Study reporting a Mediterranean diet adherence score estimate for incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: Per 2-point increment in alternate Mediterranean diet score without alcohol (aMEDr)
extraction.population: Men and women in the Netherlands Cohort Study who completed a baseline diet questionnaire

sample_size.excerpt: We examined the relation of Mediterranean diet (MD) adherence with risks of prostate and bladder cancer in the Netherlands Cohort Study (NLCS). Data were available for 58,279 men and 62,573 women, who completed a baseline questionnaire on diet and other cancer risk factors.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 58279 + 62573 = 120852

cases.excerpt: After 20.3 years of follow-up, 3,868 prostate cancer cases (advanced: 1,256) and 1,884 bladder cancer cases could be included in multivariable Cox proportional hazards analyses.

effect_size.excerpt: For bladder cancer risk, no association was observed with aMEDr [HR<sub>per 2-point increment</sub> (95% CI) = 1.00 (0.92-1.09)]. Absolute scores based on the World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research (WCRF/AICR) dietary recommendations were not associated with prostate or bladder cancer risk.

confidence_interval.excerpt: For bladder cancer risk, no association was observed with aMEDr [HR<sub>per 2-point increment</sub> (95% CI) = 1.00 (0.92-1.09)].

design.excerpt: risks of prostate and bladder cancer in the Netherlands Cohort Study (NLCS)

exposure_measurement.excerpt: who completed a baseline questionnaire on diet and other cancer risk factors. Multiple MD scores, including the alternate Mediterranean diet score without alcohol (aMEDr), were calculated

gender.excerpt: Data were available for 58,279 men and 62,573 women
